title: Ground-State Energy Solutions of the Lithium Atom: Zeroth-, First-, and Second-Order Perturbation Theory and the Variational Method
authors: Afraa Mahboubi, Büşra Gökçe Zolmaz, Devrim Karayer, Handenur Şay, Oğuzhan Kaya, Abdulkadir Senol
abstract: In this work, the ground-state energy of the lithium atom is systematically investigated using both time-independent perturbation theory and the variational method to provide a comprehensive pedagogical analysis of many-body atomic systems. The unperturbed Hamiltonian is initially constructed by neglecting electron-electron interactions, treating the system as three independent hydrogen-like electrons to yield a zeroth-order energy baseline of -275.51 eV. The antisymmetric fermionic nature of the exact wave function is rigorously enforced through the Slater determinant formalism. First-order perturbation theory is applied to evaluate static inter-electronic repulsion using exact Coulomb and exchange integrals, refining the energy state to -192.01 eV. To account for dynamical electronic correlation, second-order perturbation theory is computed numerically for virtual single-electron s-orbital transitions, leading to a total perturbative energy of -196.36 eV. A brief discussion of two-electron excitations is also included to encapsulate further physical realism within the framework. Furthermore, a non-orthogonal two-parameter variational approach is employed to model the shell-specific shielding effect. By optimizing the effective nuclear charges, the variational method establishes a superior upper bound energy of -201.187 eV. The results of both methods are comprehensively contrasted against each other and the reference baseline to provide critical insights into the nature of electron correlation and screening in multi-electron atoms.
summary: This paper calculates the ground-state energy of the lithium atom using multiple sophisticated quantum mechanical techniques. It rigorously compares results from second-order perturbation theory against a non-orthogonal variational method. The study successfully demonstrates that the variational approach provides a highly accurate upper bound, offering deep insight into electron correlation and screening effects in multi-electron atoms.
main_problem: The work systematically investigates the ground-state energy of the lithium atom by comparing results from time-independent perturbation theory and the variational method to understand electron correlation and screening in multi-electron atoms.
main_result: The non-orthogonal two-parameter variational approach established a superior upper bound energy of -201.187 eV, demonstrating better convergence than the second-order perturbation expansion.
method: The study employs Rayleigh-Schrödinger time-independent perturbation theory (up to second order) and a non-orthogonal variational method that optimizes effective nuclear charges for core and valence shells.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Lithium atom ($Z=3$) with three electrons. The Hamiltonian is treated by partitioning it into an unperturbed, independent-particle part ($\hat{H}_0$) and a perturbation term ($\hat{H}^{(1)}$) accounting for inter-electronic repulsion.
key_observables: Ground-state energy (in eV), effective nuclear charges ($\alpha$ and $ eta$), Coulomb ($J$) and Exchange ($K$) integrals.
important_parameters: The calculation relies on the non-relativistic approximation, using orbital wave functions derived from hydrogenic solutions for initial states.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include enforcing fermionic anti-symmetry via Slater determinants and restricting calculations to s-wave channels due to computational tractability in certain steps.
figures_summary: Figures compare the total ground-state energy convergence across successive perturbation orders against a reference baseline, illustrating systematic error reduction.
paper_structure: The paper builds logically by establishing a zeroth-order baseline using independent particles, then systematically applying first and second-order corrections from perturbation theory. This is contrasted with the variational method's optimization of effective charges to achieve an upper bound, culminating in a comparison of convergence rates.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed pedagogical comparison between two cornerstone techniques—perturbation theory and variational methods—for calculating correlation energy in light atoms, which is foundational knowledge for advanced AMO/many-body physics simulations.
